questions.stem: The main aim of aggregate supply (supply-side) policies is to:
options: change the cash rate so that inflation returns to the target band
balance the federal budget in every year of the economic cycle
raise the economy's productive capacity and efficiency over the long term
adjust total spending in the short term to smooth out the economic cycle
questions.explanation: Supply-side policies aim to shift long-run aggregate supply and the production possibility curve outwards. Smoothing spending over the cycle is the job of demand management through fiscal and monetary policy.

questions.stem: Microeconomic reform refers to government policies that:
options: set the cash rate in order to influence borrowing across the whole economy
fix the exchange rate to protect exporters from currency swings
improve the efficiency of individual markets, industries and firms
change total spending in the economy through the federal budget
questions.explanation: Microeconomic reform works at the level of particular markets, such as removing barriers to competition, reforming regulation or cutting tariffs. Together these reforms raise aggregate supply.

questions.stem: Supply-side policies support the goal of low and stable inflation mainly because they:
options: fix the prices of essential goods and services by regulation
let output grow faster without demand outstripping productive capacity
reduce aggregate demand directly by raising the taxes on household income
raise interest rates, which discourages borrowing and spending
questions.explanation: If capacity grows in step with spending, the economy can expand without the shortages that push prices up. Raising taxes and interest rates are demand-side tools.

questions.stem: Supply-side policies that improve workers' skills and job matching can help achieve full employment by:
options: lowering the NAIRU, so unemployment can fall without raising inflation
raising cyclical unemployment, which reduces wage pressure in the economy
increasing aggregate demand through higher government transfer payments
preventing firms from replacing workers with new technology and machines
questions.explanation: Reducing structural unemployment lowers the unemployment rate consistent with stable inflation. That lets the economy sustain lower unemployment, which demand management alone cannot achieve.

questions.stem: Supply-side policies can help external stability mainly because higher productivity:
options: raises the exchange rate, which makes Australian exports much cheaper for overseas buyers
increases foreign borrowing, which reduces the primary income deficit over time
lets the government impose tariffs on imports without breaking trade agreements
improves international competitiveness, supporting exports and import-competing firms
questions.explanation: Lower unit costs let Australian firms compete on price and quality at home and abroad, helping the trade balance over time. An appreciation makes exports dearer, not cheaper.

questions.stem: Productivity is best defined as:
options: output per unit of input, such as output per hour worked
the total value of output produced in the economy in a year
the number of people employed in a particular industry
the share of income that households spend on consumption
questions.explanation: Productivity measures how efficiently inputs are turned into output. Total output can rise simply by using more inputs, without any rise in productivity.

questions.stem: Average wages rise by 4 per cent in a year while labour productivity rises by 1.5 per cent. Unit labour costs will rise by about:
options: 4.0 per cent
1.5 per cent
2.5 per cent
5.5 per cent
questions.explanation: Unit labour costs grow by roughly wages growth minus productivity growth: 4 - 1.5 = 2.5 per cent. Faster productivity growth would hold unit costs down and improve competitiveness.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly links a supply-side policy to the type of efficiency it mainly improves?
options: Support for research and innovation: allocative efficiency only
Removing barriers to competition: none of the types of efficiency
Better transport infrastructure: lower productive efficiency
Support for research and innovation: dynamic efficiency
questions.explanation: Innovation improves the way resources adapt and new products and processes emerge over time, which is dynamic efficiency. Removing barriers to competition and better infrastructure also improve efficiency rather than reduce it.

questions.stem: Investment in freight rail and port upgrades raises productivity mainly by:
options: reducing the number of firms that need to transport goods to market
cutting the time and cost of moving goods, so firms produce and deliver more cheaply
raising the price of freight so that firms use transport less and save fuel
employing construction workers who would otherwise be producing exports
questions.explanation: Better transport infrastructure lowers firms' costs and widens the markets they can reach. Lower costs per unit of output are a productivity and competitiveness gain.

questions.stem: Governments often fund major infrastructure themselves, rather than leaving it to private firms, mainly because:
options: its benefits are widely shared and hard to charge for, so the market under-provides it
private firms are not permitted by law to own any roads, ports or communications networks
infrastructure has no effect on productivity, so private firms see no profit in it
government spending on infrastructure always pays for itself within one year
questions.explanation: Much infrastructure has public good features and positive externalities, so private investors cannot capture all the benefits. Private ownership is allowed and common in some sectors.

questions.stem: A large infrastructure program begins while the economy is already operating near full capacity. A likely short-term problem is that:
options: the project immediately lowers all firms' costs, causing deflation across the whole economy
the program reduces aggregate demand, pushing the economy into a recession
the new infrastructure shifts aggregate supply left as soon as it is announced
construction adds to aggregate demand and competes for scarce labour, adding to inflation
questions.explanation: Building infrastructure adds to spending years before the finished project lifts capacity. Timing matters: in a tight economy the demand effect can add to cost pressures in construction and beyond.

questions.stem: Which is the best way to judge whether a proposed infrastructure project is a sound supply-side policy?
options: Whether it will employ more construction workers than any rival project
Whether its cost is larger than the cost of other proposed projects
A cost-benefit analysis comparing its long-term benefits with all its costs
Whether it can be completed before the next federal election is held
questions.explanation: Cost-benefit analysis tests whether a project's benefits, such as time and cost savings, exceed its full costs, including the opportunity cost of the funds. Poorly chosen projects can waste resources.

questions.stem: Investment in high-speed broadband networks is expected to raise productivity mainly by:
options: raising the cost of online services so that firms invest in buildings
reducing competition between firms located in different regions
increasing the number of hours each employee must work each week
letting firms adopt digital tools and reach customers at lower cost
questions.explanation: Fast, reliable connections let firms use cloud services, trade online and work remotely, cutting costs and widening markets. That raises output per unit of input.

questions.stem: Spending on education and training is a supply-side policy because it:
options: reduces the number of people in the labour force permanently
lowers the cash rate by reducing the federal budget deficit
improves the quality of labour, raising output per worker
raises household spending on consumer goods in the short term
questions.explanation: Education and training build human capital, so workers can produce more and adapt to new technology. That lifts productivity and productive capacity.

questions.stem: Funding extra training places in occupations with skill shortages is designed mainly to reduce:
options: structural unemployment caused by a mismatch of skills
cyclical unemployment caused by weak aggregate demand in a downturn
seasonal unemployment in tourism and agriculture
frictional unemployment from people changing jobs
questions.explanation: Training lets unemployed or displaced workers gain skills that growing industries need, closing the gap between workers' skills and available jobs. Cyclical unemployment is addressed by demand management.

questions.stem: Subsidised childcare can raise aggregate supply mainly because it:
options: allows more parents to work or work longer hours, raising participation
reduces the number of childcare workers employed in the economy
lowers the participation rate by encouraging parents to stay home
raises the price of childcare so that providers expand their centres
questions.explanation: Lower childcare costs make paid work more worthwhile for parents, especially second earners, lifting the participation rate and the economy's labour supply.

questions.stem: A limitation of education and training as a supply-side policy is that:
options: it raises inflation immediately because newly trained workers demand higher wages
it has no effect on productivity because skills cannot be measured
it works only during recessions and has no effect during booms
the costs fall on the budget now, while productivity gains take years to appear
questions.explanation: Students take years to complete courses and enter the workforce, so the benefits are delayed and hard to attribute. This time lag can make such policies less attractive politically.

questions.stem: Governments support research and development (R&D) mainly because R&D:
options: reduces aggregate supply by using resources that could produce goods today
is a public good that private firms are not permitted to undertake
creates benefits for other firms and society that the investing firm cannot capture
always earns the investing firm a guaranteed profit within the first year
questions.explanation: Knowledge spreads to other firms, so the private return to R&D is less than the social return and the market under-invests. Tax incentives and grants aim to correct this positive externality.

questions.stem: A tax incentive that lets firms claim extra deductions for eligible R&D spending aims to:
options: reduce the number of new products so that existing firms face less competition
lower the after-tax cost of R&D, encouraging innovation and dynamic efficiency
raise the after-tax cost of R&D, so that only the most profitable projects proceed
replace private R&D spending with government research in public universities
questions.explanation: Reducing the effective cost of research encourages firms to undertake more of it, leading to new products and processes. That lifts productivity growth over time.

questions.stem: Innovation raises productivity when new ideas are:
options: commercialised and spread widely through firms across the economy
kept secret indefinitely within the single firm that developed them
protected from use by any firm for as long as possible
limited to research laboratories and never used in production
questions.explanation: Productivity gains come when inventions are turned into products and processes and adopted by many firms. Policies that support commercialisation and the spread of technology therefore matter as much as research itself.

questions.stem: A government gives grants to help universities and start-ups turn research into new products. When evaluating this policy, the strongest concern would be that:
options: new products always reduce employment across the whole economy
innovation cannot affect productivity or international competitiveness
public funds may back projects that fail, with a high opportunity cost
the grants will immediately reduce aggregate supply in the economy
questions.explanation: Innovation is risky, and governments may pick projects that do not succeed, while the money could have been used elsewhere. Good evaluation weighs these risks against the spillover benefits of successful ideas.

questions.stem: Deregulation means:
options: introducing new government rules to control the prices that are charged by private firms
transferring private businesses into government ownership to improve services
increasing tariffs on imports to give local firms more room to compete
removing or reducing government rules that restrict competition or add needless costs
questions.explanation: Deregulation aims to free markets from unnecessary restrictions, such as limits on entry or excessive compliance costs. It is meant to increase competition and efficiency.

questions.stem: Reducing the paperwork and approval times that businesses face raises aggregate supply mainly by:
options: reducing the number of firms that can legally enter each market
lowering compliance costs, so firms can produce more at each price level
raising compliance costs, so that firms invest more in administrative staff
lowering aggregate demand, so the price level falls across the economy
questions.explanation: Red tape takes time and money that could otherwise go into production. Cutting unnecessary compliance shifts aggregate supply to the right.

questions.stem: Australia's financial deregulation in the 1980s, including floating the dollar and allowing more banks to compete, was intended mainly to:
options: reduce the flow of foreign capital into Australia
increase competition and efficiency in the financial system
protect the existing Australian banks from new foreign competition
fix interest rates at a level set by the government
questions.explanation: Removing controls on interest rates, exchange rates and bank entry was designed to make finance more competitive and responsive. It opened Australia to capital flows rather than restricting them.

questions.stem: National Competition Policy, agreed by Australian governments in the mid-1990s, aimed mainly to:
options: raise tariffs to protect Australian manufacturers from overseas rivals
fix prices in electricity and gas markets to protect households
merge competing firms into larger national monopolies
open government utilities and protected markets to greater competition
questions.explanation: National Competition Policy applied competition principles to government businesses and reviewed laws that restricted competition, for example in electricity, gas and transport. The aim was lower costs and better services.

questions.stem: A state government removes the cap on taxi licences and allows rideshare services to operate. The most likely outcome is:
options: gains for licence holders, as their licences become more valuable
lower fares and more choice for passengers, but losses for licence holders
higher fares and less choice, as fewer firms now compete for passengers
no change in fares, because rideshare services do not compete with taxis
questions.explanation: Removing the entry restriction increases competition, pushing fares down and improving service. The value of existing licences falls, showing how reform creates losers as well as winners.

questions.stem: A risk of going too far with deregulation is that:
options: it prevents new firms from entering markets that were previously regulated
removing important rules can allow market failures such as consumer harm or financial instability
competition always falls when rules are removed, so prices rise in every market that is deregulated
deregulation always reduces productivity because firms no longer face any rules
questions.explanation: Some regulation corrects genuine market failures, such as asymmetric information or risky lending. The aim is better regulation that keeps those protections while removing unnecessary costs.

questions.stem: Reducing tariffs is often included in microeconomic reform because it:
options: reduces competition so that local firms gain economies of scale
exposes local firms to competition and lowers the cost of imported inputs
raises import prices so that local firms can expand their market share
raises government revenue, which funds new infrastructure projects
questions.explanation: Lower tariffs push protected firms to become more efficient and give other firms cheaper inputs, shifting resources to industries where Australia is more competitive.

questions.stem: Which indicator would best show whether supply-side policies are lifting the efficiency of the economy over time?
options: The size of the federal budget deficit
Growth in multifactor productivity
The monthly change in retail sales
The quarterly change in the cash rate
questions.explanation: Multifactor productivity measures output relative to both labour and capital inputs, so it captures improvements in how efficiently resources are used. Retail sales and the cash rate reflect demand conditions.

questions.stem: Supply-side reforms are often hard to implement because of political constraints. This is mainly because:
options: the costs fall on visible groups who resist, while the benefits are spread thinly
the benefits are immediate and obvious, so voters see no need for any further change
they require the Reserve Bank's approval before they can be passed
they always reduce economic growth in the year they are introduced
questions.explanation: Workers and firms in affected industries lose quickly and lobby hard, while the gains to consumers and the wider economy are diffuse and slow to appear. That makes reform politically difficult.

questions.stem: Structural adjustment assistance, such as retraining and relocation support, is provided alongside microeconomic reform mainly to:
options: reverse the reform if unemployment rises in the first year
help workers displaced by reform move into growing industries
stop firms from closing in industries that have lost protection
raise tariffs again in industries that have shed workers
questions.explanation: Reform shifts resources between industries, which can leave some workers unemployed. Assistance eases the equity cost and speeds the move of labour to where it is more productive.

questions.stem: Which statement best compares supply-side policies with demand management policies?
options: Both act only on aggregate supply, but use different policy instruments
Supply-side policies work slowly on capacity; demand policies act faster on spending
Supply-side policies act quickly on spending; demand policies work slowly on capacity
Both act only on aggregate demand, but over different lengths of time
questions.explanation: Fiscal and monetary policy change spending within months to stabilise the cycle, while supply-side policies take years to raise productive capacity. Used together, they aim for sustainable, non-inflationary growth.

questions.stem: Productivity growth in Australia slows even though the government has increased spending on supply-side programs. Which explanation best reflects a limitation of these policies?
options: Supply-side programs always raise productivity within one year, so the data must be wrong
Government spending on supply-side programs reduces aggregate demand, which then lowers productivity
Productivity cannot be measured, so it is impossible to say whether policies are working
Global influences, such as a worldwide slowdown in technology diffusion, can offset domestic reforms
questions.explanation: Productivity depends partly on global trends in technology and trade that a single government cannot control, and reforms take time to work. Evaluating a policy means allowing for these outside influences.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a supply-side policy rather than a demand management policy?
options: A temporary rise in income tax rates to slow spending
Funding to expand vocational training in skill-shortage trades
A cut in the cash rate to encourage borrowing and spending
A one-off cash payment to households during a downturn
questions.explanation: Training raises the quality of labour and the economy's capacity over time. Changing the cash rate, one-off payments and temporary tax changes aim to shift aggregate demand in the short term.

questions.stem: A government justifies a supply-side reform on efficiency grounds, but critics argue it will widen inequality between regions. This illustrates that:
options: efficiency and equity always improve together under reform
regional inequality can be fixed only by monetary policy
economic policies involve trade-offs between efficiency and equity
supply-side policies have no effect on how income is distributed
questions.explanation: A reform can raise productivity overall while concentrating losses in particular regions or groups. Governments weigh such trade-offs and may combine reform with targeted assistance.
